paragraphs.text: A land creature is a permanent that is both a land and a creature . They are most often lands that can self- animate , which are sometimes referred to as "manlands", "landfolk", or "creature lands", with the last being the preferred term in Wizards of the Coast 's style guide. One card, Dryad Arbor , is a land and a creature at all times and in all zones , which creates unintuitive rules interactions.

The earliest self-animating land was Mishra's Factory ( Antiquities ). Such cards are popular and tend to be powerful. They provide resilience against both mana flood and mana screw , allow their controller to change tempo , and can avoid certain kinds of removal . The presence of creature lands in a metagame encourages higher land counts in deckbuilding , which promotes midrange and control decks .

Mishra's Factory inspired a mono-colored cycle of animating lands in Urza's Legacy and an allied color cycle in Worldwake . For Worldwake , those lands provided the set's theme, "When Lands Attack." The second Zendikar block, Battle for Zendikar block , contains an enemy colored cycle to complement Worldwake . The Lost Caverns of Ixalan , and Wilds of Eldraine has a new mega-cycle of two-color lands with the theme name of "Restless", split between ally and enemy cycles respectively. Adventures in the Forgotten Realms has a monocolored cycle with a fast land clause.
Creature lands most often animate until the end of turn , but exceptions like Soulstone Sanctuary exist.

The ability to animate lands, broadly, is primary for green and secondary for red . It is tertiary for the other colors, which most often see the mechanic in cycles. It can be done through several methods: an Aura, a counter with a built-in ability (thus far only with an awakening counter ), or an ability that changes its type to creature, while often still being a land. The latter may be a 0/0 with +1/+1 counters or have a set power and toughness. In contrast to creature lands, external animators will usually animate permanently, with a few exceptions for repeatable animators. Like other animate effects, it is often used as a way to utilize excess mana on the board. As it would be a liability to lose a land to removal or combat early in the game, animation effects can sometimes be cheaper than the size would imply, or be on rate with a clause that mitigates the player losing the land.

The awaken and earthbend keywords also can animate lands permanently. Both of these use the 0/0 with counters method, and earthbending also has a clause that returns the land to the battlefield if the land is exiled or destroyed.

Only one tournament-legal card, Dryad Arbor ( Future Sight ), has both land and creature types at all times. It derives the activated ability " : Add " from its Forest land type, and the characteristic-defining ability shown on its original printing has since been removed and replaced by a color indicator via errata . Because the Oracle reference contains no rules text, it is now a vanilla creature.

Unlike animated lands, having both types in all zones causes unintuitive interactions. Dryad Arbor must be played as a land drop , rather than cast , and does not benefit from abilities that allow creatures to be cast as though they had flash , or from other zones. Because it is a creature and is affected by summoning sickness , it cannot be tapped for mana on the turn it enters the battlefield.

New mechanics that affect either creatures or lands have a chance to cause problems with Dryad Arbor . The existence of Dryad Arbor delayed errata for three other cards, which eventually received functional errata and no longer interact with Dryad Arbor . Because of the rules oddities, additional cards that are lands and creatures in all zones are unlikely. However, one Mystery Booster playtest card , Jasconian Isle , further complicates the gameplay of the land creature type combination by adding abilities inspired by Island Fish Jasconius .

The From the Vault: Realms printing of Dryad Arbor has only a large green mana symbol in its text box, like typical basic Forests. That resemblance led to a high-profile misplay during a 2018 tournament. Afterwards, the Tournament Rules were updated to require that all creatures, regardless of their other types, must be kept together on the battlefield, as had been suggested by multiple commentators. Mark Rosewater considers the layout used for that printing to be a mistake.

The release of The Brothers' War and The Brothers' War commander decks saw the introduction of the Forest Dryad token. Aside from being a token , it functions identically to Dryad Arbor , avoiding the card's issues as most of the problems are with non-battlefield behaviors. The token is also produced by a card in MH3 Commander and Mystery Booster Commander Edition each.
